---
title: "Off-policy and on-policy"
subtitle: "Learning from the teacher's text, or from your own"
---

{{< include /_setup.qmd >}}

B and C learn from text the teacher wrote: they are **off-policy**. At test time, though, the student
writes its own answers, one token after another, each conditioned on its own earlier tokens. One
early slip, a wrong function name or a missing argument, puts it in a place the teacher's text never
went, and it has never learned how to recover. This mismatch is called *exposure bias*.

An **on-policy** method trains on the student's own attempts. In D, at every step:

1. the student writes an answer to a training query (sampling at temperature 1);
2. the teacher reads that answer and gives its probability for every next token, at every
   position;
3. the student is pushed toward the teacher's distribution, on its own text.

Unlike reinforcement learning, which gets one reward per answer, every token gets feedback, so a
wrong answer still says where it went wrong.

::: {.column-margin}
[Thinking Machines, 2025](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/on-policy-distillation/);
[GKD, Agarwal et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13649).
:::

## Forward and reverse KL

The loss turns around too. D uses the **reverse KL**, from the student's distribution $q$ to the
teacher's $p$:

$$\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \sum_v q(v) \log \frac{q(v)}{p(v)}.$$

The forward KL of C, $\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q)$, is large wherever the teacher puts probability and
the student doesn't: it makes the student *cover* every option the teacher considers. The reverse
KL is large wherever the student puts probability and the teacher doesn't: it makes the student
avoid what the teacher would never write, and settle on what the teacher prefers. For a small
student that can't match everything, that is usually the better trade.

## What it costs

The teacher has to score every answer the student writes, during training, so D runs both models
and a sampling engine at once. On the 12 GB card: TRL's `DistillationTrainer`, the student sampling
in vLLM next to training, and the 2B in the same process. D's full epoch took
`{python} f"{last['D']['gpu_hours']:.1f}"` GPU-hours, against
`{python} f"{last['B']['gpu_hours']:.1f}"` for B's full epoch, the teacher's pass included.
